title: Common Equality Bugs
summary: Catalog, debug, and prevent the most treacherous equality bugs in Java: null dereferences, accidental overloads, inheritance asymmetry, and float comparisons.
learningObjectives: Recognize the top 5 equality anti-patterns in enterprise Java codebases
Prevent NullPointerExceptions in equals() when fields contain null values
Eliminate inheritance asymmetry bugs using exact class matching (getClass() vs instanceof)
Compare floating-point NaN and -0.0 fields accurately using Double.compare
expectedOutcomes: You can audit any equals() implementation and immediately pinpoint edge-case vulnerabilities
You write robust, crash-proof equality logic that handles nulls, inheritance, and floats safely

activities.title: Practical Context: Diagnosing Subversive Equality Pitfalls

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: At airport border control, an officer has a strict checklist: (1) Is the passport physically present? (If missing, reject immediately—don't try to open a non-existent booklet!). (2) Is this document actually a passport, or a library card? (Check document type!). (3) Compare name, photo, and birthdate. If the officer tried to inspect a passenger who didn't exist or compared a dog license to a human passport, the system would collapse in chaos.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In software, failing to check for null causes a `NullPointerException` (inspecting a missing passport). Failing to verify exact type causes a `ClassCastException` (treating a library card as a passport).
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: A defensive equals() method checks preconditions (identity, nullity, type) before attempting to read field values.

activities.content:
Equality implementation is deceptively simple, yet subtle edge cases routinely cause production regressions.

Whether checking subclasses, handling mutable fields inside collections, or accidentally overloading instead of overriding, equality anti-patterns are difficult to diagnose once deployed.

Understanding these pitfalls ensures bulletproof domain implementations.

activities.title: Common Equality Anti-Patterns: getClass() vs instanceof and Mutability Traps
Inheritance Asymmetry Breakdown: Point and ColorPoint
activities.explanation: Illustrates why instanceof in instantiable class hierarchies breaks the mathematical symmetry contract. Using getClass() != obj.getClass() fixes this permanently.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `p.equals(cp)` checks `cp instanceof Point`, which is `true`, and compares coordinates (matches).
`cp.equals(p)` checks `p instanceof ColorPoint`, which is `false`, returning `false`.
Symmetry requires `p.equals(cp) == cp.equals(p)`. The contract is shattered.
Using `getClass() != obj.getClass()` in Point makes `p.equals(cp)` return false, preserving symmetry.

activities.title: Hardening Against Null Fields with Objects.equals()
activities.explanation: Objects.equals gracefully handles combinations of null and non-null values without crashing.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: All edge cases are handled cleanly and safely.

questions.question: What happens if a field is null and you execute `this.field.equals(other.field)`?
questions.explanation: Invoking .equals() directly on a null reference throws a NullPointerException at runtime.

questions.question: What is the simplest way to compare two object references for equality while protecting against nulls?
questions.explanation: java.util.Objects.equals(a, b) safely checks identity and handles nulls before calling equals.

questions.question: Why does using `instanceof` in an instantiable parent class often violate the Symmetry contract?
options: Because a parent instance can match the subclass type in parent.equals(child), but child.equals(parent) rejects the parent
Because instanceof is slower than reflection
Because the compiler forbids instanceof in equals
Because instanceof only works on interfaces
questions.explanation: If a subclass adds state, parent.equals(child) will ignore the state and return true, while child.equals(parent) will return false.

questions.question: How should double and float primitive fields be compared in equals()?
questions.explanation: Double.compare handles NaN == NaN (true) and -0.0 vs +0.0 (distinguished) correctly.

questions.question: What subtle bug occurs when comparing array fields with `this.arr.equals(other.arr)`?
options: It compares the memory address of the arrays instead of their contents
It only compares the first element
questions.explanation: Arrays inherit Object.equals directly and do NOT override it to compare elements. Use Arrays.equals() instead.

questions.question: What happens if you write `public boolean equals(MyType obj)` without the `@Override` annotation?
options: You accidentally create an overload; methods that expect equals(Object) will never call your method
The compiler automatically fixes the signature
questions.explanation: Without @Override, you create an overload that is completely ignored by collections like ArrayList.contains().

questions.question: What does Joshua Bloch recommend if you want to extend a class and add a value component while preserving equals?
questions.answer: Favor composition over inheritance: make the parent class a private field of the new class rather than extending it.
options: Favor composition over inheritance: make the parent class a field of the new class
Use reflection to alter superclass fields
questions.explanation: Composition allows adding new fields without breaking Liskov substitution or equals contract symmetry.

questions.question: What should `anyNonNullObject.equals(null)` return according to the Object contract?
questions.explanation: The non-nullity rule requires returning false when compared to null, never throwing an exception.

questions.question: Why is `if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass()) return false;` safer than `!(obj instanceof Foo)` for concrete classes?
options: It guarantees both objects belong to the exact same runtime class, eliminating subclass asymmetry
questions.explanation: Comparing getClass() ensures that only instances of the exact same concrete class can be considered equal.

questions.question: Can `getClass()` check throw a NullPointerException in `if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass())`?
options: No, because short-circuit evaluation (`obj == null ||`) halts before `obj.getClass()` is evaluated if obj is null
questions.explanation: The short-circuit OR operator `||` guarantees that if `obj == null`, the second operand is never evaluated.

questions.question: What is the 'Point and ColorPoint' problem and why is it so famous in OOP literature?
questions.answer: It is Joshua Bloch's fundamental proof that it is impossible to extend an instantiable class and add a value field while preserving the equals contract (symmetry and transitivity). If you check `instanceof Point`, `point.equals(colorPoint)` returns true while `colorPoint.equals(point)` returns false (symmetry broken). If you try to fix symmetry by ignoring color when comparing ColorPoint with Point, transitivity is broken: RedPoint(1,2) equals Point(1,2), and Point(1,2) equals BluePoint(1,2), but RedPoint does NOT equal BluePoint!
questions.expectedAnswer: It is Joshua Bloch's fundamental proof that it is impossible to extend an instantiable class and add a value field while preserving the equals contract (symmetry and transitivity). If you check `instanceof Point`, `point.equals(colorPoint)` returns true while `colorPoint.equals(point)` returns false (symmetry broken). If you try to fix symmetry by ignoring color when comparing ColorPoint with Point, transitivity is broken: RedPoint(1,2) equals Point(1,2), and Point(1,2) equals BluePoint(1,2), but RedPoint does NOT equal BluePoint!
questions.keyTakeaway: Adding value fields via subclassing inherently breaks symmetry or transitivity. Use composition instead.
keyPoints: Adding value fields via subclassing inherently breaks symmetry or transitivity. Use composition instead.

questions.question: When IS `instanceof` acceptable in an equals() method?
questions.answer: `instanceof` is acceptable and preferred when implementing equals() for a standard **Interface** (e.g. `java.util.Set`, `java.util.List`, `java.util.Map`). `Set.equals()` specifies that ANY implementation of Set with the same elements is equal, allowing `HashSet` and `TreeSet` to be logically equal.
questions.expectedAnswer: `instanceof` is acceptable and preferred when implementing equals() for a standard **Interface** (e.g. `java.util.Set`, `java.util.List`, `java.util.Map`). `Set.equals()` specifies that ANY implementation of Set with the same elements is equal, allowing `HashSet` and `TreeSet` to be logically equal.
questions.keyTakeaway: instanceof is appropriate for interface contracts where cross-implementation equality is explicitly defined.
keyPoints: instanceof is appropriate for interface contracts where cross-implementation equality is explicitly defined.

questions.question: How do you test that an equals() method satisfies the 5 contract properties in unit tests?
questions.answer: Use testing libraries like `EqualsVerifier` (`EqualsVerifier.forClass(MyClass.class).verify()`). It automatically tests reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, consistency, non-nullity, hash code alignment, and inheritance edge cases.
questions.expectedAnswer: Use testing libraries like `EqualsVerifier` (`EqualsVerifier.forClass(MyClass.class).verify()`). It automatically tests reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, consistency, non-nullity, hash code alignment, and inheritance edge cases.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use EqualsVerifier to automate testing of all mathematical equals/hashCode contract rules.
keyPoints: Use EqualsVerifier to automate testing of all mathematical equals/hashCode contract rules.

questions.question: Why should you never write `new URL("http://...").equals(...)` in latency-sensitive code?
questions.answer: Java's `java.net.URL.equals()` method performs a blocking DNS lookup to resolve the host IP address! If the network is down or slow, calling `.equals()` on a URL will freeze your thread for several seconds. Always use `java.net.URI` instead, which compares strings without DNS lookups.
questions.expectedAnswer: Java's `java.net.URL.equals()` method performs a blocking DNS lookup to resolve the host IP address! If the network is down or slow, calling `.equals()` on a URL will freeze your thread for several seconds. Always use `java.net.URI` instead, which compares strings without DNS lookups.
questions.keyTakeaway: java.net.URL.equals performs a blocking DNS lookup; use java.net.URI instead.
keyPoints: java.net.URL.equals performs a blocking DNS lookup; use java.net.URI instead.

questions.question: How does `BigDecimal.equals()` differ from `BigDecimal.compareTo()`?
questions.answer: `BigDecimal.equals()` checks value AND scale: `new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` returns `false` (scales differ)! In contrast, `compareTo()` compares mathematical numerical values: `new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00")) == 0` is `true`.
questions.expectedAnswer: `BigDecimal.equals()` checks value AND scale: `new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` returns `false` (scales differ)! In contrast, `compareTo()` compares mathematical numerical values: `new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00")) == 0` is `true`.
questions.keyTakeaway: BigDecimal.equals considers scale; BigDecimal.compareTo considers only numerical value.
keyPoints: BigDecimal.equals considers scale; BigDecimal.compareTo considers only numerical value.

questions.question: What is the danger of writing equals() using reflection (e.g. `EqualsBuilder.reflectionEquals`)?
questions.answer: Reflection-based equals has significant performance overhead (10-50x slower), breaks encapsulation by accessing private fields directly, and can fail under modern Java modularity (Java 9+ strong encapsulation) unless packages are opened.
questions.expectedAnswer: Reflection-based equals has significant performance overhead (10-50x slower), breaks encapsulation by accessing private fields directly, and can fail under modern Java modularity (Java 9+ strong encapsulation) unless packages are opened.
questions.keyTakeaway: Reflection-based equals is slow, fragile, and breaches module boundaries.
keyPoints: Reflection-based equals is slow, fragile, and breaches module boundaries.

activities.title: Common Equality Bugs Checklist
items: I use Objects.equals(f1, f2) to prevent NullPointerExceptions on null fields.
I always use parameter type Object and annotate with @Override.
I use getClass() != obj.getClass() on concrete classes to prevent inheritance asymmetry.
I use Double.compare and Float.compare for floating-point fields.
I use Arrays.equals() or Arrays.deepEquals() for array fields.
I ensure x.equals(null) returns false without throwing an exception.
I avoid subclassing instantiable classes when adding state (I use composition).
I know why java.net.URL.equals is dangerous (blocking DNS resolution).
I know why BigDecimal.equals checks scale while compareTo checks value.
I use automated tools like EqualsVerifier in unit test suites.

practiceProblems.title: Null-Safe User Profile Equality
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Fix the `UserProfile` class so it does not throw `NullPointerException` when `nickname` is null. Use `java.util.Objects.equals` to compare `userId` and `nickname` safely.

practiceProblems.title: Fixing Symmetry Violation in Subclass Hierarchy
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Fix the asymmetry bug between `BaseToken` and `ExpiringToken` from scratch:
1. Class `BaseToken`: holds `protected String tokenId`. Constructor initializes it.
   - Implement `equals(Object obj)` using exact class matching: `if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass()) return false;`.
   - Two BaseTokens are equal if their tokenId matches.
   - Implement `hashCode()` using `Objects.hash(tokenId)`.
2. Class `ExpiringToken` extending `BaseToken`: holds `private long expiryTimestamp`.
   - Constructor initializes tokenId and expiryTimestamp.
   - Implement `equals(Object obj)` using exact class matching (`getClass() != obj.getClass()`), comparing tokenId and expiryTimestamp.
   - Implement `hashCode()` using `Objects.hash(tokenId, expiryTimestamp)`.
3. In `Main`, create base = BaseToken("T100") and expiring = ExpiringToken("T100", 5000L).
4. Verify that symmetry is preserved: print `base.equals(expiring)` (false) and `expiring.equals(base)` (false).
hints: By using getClass() != obj.getClass(), base sees expiring.getClass() is ExpiringToken, so it returns false.

practiceProblems.title: Robust Floating-Point NaN and Zero Equality
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a financial rate class handling floating-point edge cases from scratch:
1. Class `InterestRate`: holds `private double annualPercentageRate`.
   - Constructor initializes it.
   - Override `equals(Object obj)`: use `Double.compare(this.annualPercentageRate, other.annualPercentageRate) == 0`.
   - Override `hashCode()`: return `Double.hashCode(annualPercentageRate)`.
2. In `Main`, test:
   - Create r1 with `Double.NaN` and r2 with `Double.NaN`.
   - Print `'NaN rates equal: ' + r1.equals(r2)` (true, Double.compare treats NaN == NaN as true!).
   - Create r3 with `0.0` and r4 with `-0.0`.
   - Print `'Positive vs Negative zero equal: ' + r3.equals(r4)` (false, Double.compare distinguishes -0.0 from +0.0!).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
NaN rates equal: true
Positive vs Negative zero equal: false

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Accidental Parameter Overload with Specific Class
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A developer wrote `public boolean equals(CustomerKey other)` instead of `public boolean equals(Object obj)`. Fix the class to properly override `Object.equals(Object)`, add `@Override`, and follow the 4-step recipe.

practiceProblems.title: Comprehensive Defense-in-Depth Entity Equality Auditor
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an entity class incorporating every single defensive equality practice from scratch:
1. Class `AuditRecord`: 
   - Fields: `private final String recordId`, `private final double transactionAmount`, `private final String[] tags` (can be null), `private final String metadata` (can be null).
   - Constructor initializes all four.
   - Implement `equals(Object obj)` adhering to all rules:
     - Check identity (`this == obj`).
     - Check `obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass()`.
     - Compare `recordId` using `Objects.equals`.
     - Compare `transactionAmount` using `Double.compare`.
     - Compare `tags` array using `java.util.Arrays.equals`.
     - Compare `metadata` using `Objects.equals`.
   - Implement `hashCode()`:
     - Use `Objects.hash(recordId, transactionAmount, Arrays.hashCode(tags), metadata)`.
2. In `Main`, test:
   - r1 = AuditRecord("REC-1", 150.0, new String[]{"finance", "q4"}, null)
   - r2 = AuditRecord("REC-1", 150.0, new String[]{"finance", "q4"}, null)
   - r3 = AuditRecord("REC-1", 150.0, new String[]{"audit"}, null)
3. Verify:
   - Print `r1.equals(r2)` (true)
   - Print `r1.equals(r3)` (false, different tags array)
   - Print `r1.equals(null)` (false)
   - Print `r1.hashCode() == r2.hashCode()` (true)
hints: Arrays.hashCode(tags) properly incorporates array content into hashCode.
